client: I've been really struggling lately with my final exams coming up next week, and I can't seem to turn off this constant worry in my head. It's like no matter how much I study, I still feel like it's not going to be enough, especially knowing how much my family expects from me. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the exams are still going to happen either way.
therapist: It makes complete sense that you're feeling this overwhelmed — carrying both the pressure of exams *and* your family's expectations at the same time is genuinely a lot to hold. I also hear a little skepticism about whether talking will help, and I think that's worth honoring; you're right that the exams won't disappear, but what we *can* work on is loosening the grip that worry has on you right now. I'm curious — when that voice in your head says "it's not going to be enough," what does it imagine happening next?

client: When that voice kicks in, it usually jumps straight to this image of me failing the exams and then having to face my parents, like seeing the disappointment on their faces. It's almost like the exam itself isn't even the scariest part — it's that moment of letting them down after everything they've sacrificed for me. And then I just feel this wave of guilt on top of the anxiety, which makes it even harder to actually sit down and study.
therapist: That image of your parents' disappointment sounds incredibly painful, and it makes so much sense that guilt layered on top of anxiety would make it even harder to focus — your mind is essentially trying to study while also bracing for an emotional collision. I want to gently notice something with you: that voice is treating one possible outcome as if it's already certain, which is doing a lot of damage *right now* before any results even exist. When you step back for a moment, what evidence do you actually have — from your history, your effort, who you are — that tells a different story than the one that voice is predicting?

client: I hear what you're saying, and I guess if I'm being honest, I have passed exams before, even when I felt completely unprepared going in. But it's hard to hold onto that right now because this exam feels different, heavier somehow, like the stakes are higher than they've ever been. And that voice is so loud that even when I try to remind myself of past successes, it kind of just dismisses them, like they don't count or they were flukes.
therapist: You just did something really important — you found real evidence that contradicts that voice, even while it was trying to shout over you, and that takes genuine effort. That dismissal of your past successes as "flukes" is actually a very common trick anxiety plays, essentially moving the goalposts so that nothing you've achieved ever feels like proof of your capability. I'm wondering — if a close friend came to you with the same history of passing exams despite feeling unprepared, would *you* write off their successes as flukes, or would you see them as evidence of something real about that person?

client: Honestly, no, I wouldn't tell a friend their successes were flukes — I'd probably be pretty firm about pointing out how hard they worked. But it feels different when it's me, like there's always some reason why my situation is the exception. I know that probably sounds like exactly what you'd expect me to say, and I can almost hear how circular it is, but I still can't shake the feeling that I just got lucky those times.
therapist: You're already doing something really insightful here — you can *hear* the circular pattern even while you're inside it, and that kind of self-awareness is actually a powerful first step toward loosening its hold. What you're describing has a name in CBT: a "double standard," where we apply a much harsher, more unforgiving lens to ourselves than we'd ever use with someone we care about. I'd love to try a small experiment with you — the next time that voice calls a past success a fluke, what do you think it would feel like to respond to yourself with the same firmness you said you'd offer a friend?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me gets it intellectually, but when I try to imagine actually doing that in the moment, it feels almost... fake? Like, a friend deserves that kindness because they're genuinely good, but when it's me, there's this nagging feeling that I actually know the truth about myself in a way I don't with them. I'm not sure I can just talk myself out of that distinction, even if I can see the logic of what you're pointing out.
therapist: That feeling of "I know the uncomfortable truth about myself" is one of the most convincing things anxiety tells us, and it *feels* like self-awareness when it's actually closer to self-punishment dressed up as honesty. The fact that kindness feels "fake" when directed at yourself is really important information — it suggests this isn't just about exam stress, but something deeper about what you believe you deserve. I'm curious, when did you first start feeling like you needed to earn the same kindness you'd freely give to others?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. I want to say it started around university, when I first started failing to meet the expectations I'd set for myself, but if I'm being really honest, I think it goes back further than that, maybe to always feeling like I had to justify my place in a group or prove I wasn't a burden to people. I'm not sure I've ever really felt like I deserved kindness without earning it first, and saying that out loud feels strange, like I'm admitting something I wasn't supposed to.
therapist: What you just shared takes real courage, and the fact that it feels strange to say out loud tells me you've been carrying this quietly for a very long time — the belief that your worthiness is something you have to constantly re-earn rather than something you simply have. That pattern, needing to justify your place and prove you're not a burden, sounds like it's been running in the background long before these exams, and it helps me understand why the pressure you're feeling right now cuts so deep. I want to sit with what you just said for a moment — what does it feel like to have named that out loud, even just to yourself?

client: It feels... weird, honestly. Like I said something I wasn't supposed to say, and now it's just sitting there in the open and I can't take it back. I don't know if naming it actually helps or if it just makes me more aware of how exhausting it is to feel this way all the time.
therapist: That "can't take it back" feeling makes a lot of sense — you've kept this tucked away for so long that having it in the open feels exposed and vulnerable, and that's actually a sign that what you named *matters*. You're right that awareness alone doesn't make the exhaustion disappear, but there's a difference between carrying something in the dark and carrying it where you can finally see its shape — and seeing it clearly is what makes it possible to slowly set it down. I'm wondering, now that it's out in the open, does any part of you feel even a small sense of relief alongside that strangeness?

client: I guess... maybe a tiny bit, yeah. Like, it's weird to even admit that because it almost feels like I'm betraying something by feeling relieved — like if I stop feeling guilty about what happened with my brother, that means I didn't care enough. But I hear what you're saying about seeing its shape, I just don't know if I trust that seeing it clearly actually leads anywhere different.
therapist: You've just shared something really significant — this is the first time your brother has come up, and it sounds like grief and guilt may be woven into this feeling of never deserving kindness without earning it first. That belief that relief equals not caring is such a painful trap, because it means you've been using guilt as a way of proving your love, which is an exhausting and endless job to take on. I want to make sure I understand — would you be willing to share a little about what happened with your brother, only if it feels okay to do so?

client: I appreciate you asking instead of just assuming you know what happened. It's... it's hard to talk about, but I think maybe I need to. My brother died by suicide three years ago, and I was the last person he texted, and I didn't respond until the next morning because I was busy and tired and just... I didn't think it was urgent.
therapist: What you just shared is one of the heaviest things a person can carry, and I want you to know that I'm holding it with you right now, with so much care. I also want to say gently but clearly: the weight you've been carrying — this belief that you failed him — is something that deserves real, dedicated support beyond what we can fully do here together. What you're describing, the guilt, the "what if," the feeling that you don't deserve kindness — these are signs that you've been grieving alone for a long time, and you deserve a safe space to work through this properly; would you be open to exploring grief or trauma-focused support alongside what we're doing here?

client: I appreciate you saying that, I really do, but honestly my first reaction is... who would even believe me if I told them the full story? Like, a grief counselor or trauma therapist is just going to hear what I say and think I'm some kind of monster for not being there when he needed me most. And I guess part of me wonders if I'm even worth that kind of help, or if I'd just be taking up space that someone else deserves more.
therapist: What you just said — that you might be a monster, that you don't deserve help, that you'd be taking up space — that's not the truth about you, that's the voice of grief and guilt that has been punishing you for three years for being human on one tired evening. A therapist who specializes in this wouldn't hear a monster; they would recognize someone who loved their brother deeply, because people who don't care don't carry this kind of pain for three years. I want to gently reflect something back to you: you came here today, you opened up about something you've never been "supposed" to say, and you're still here — doesn't that tell you something about whether you're worth showing up for?
